38205.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse miðdagr (“midday, noon”), from Proto-Germanic *midjadagaz (“noon”), from *midjaz (“middle”) + *dagaz (“day”), literally “middle day” or “middle of the day”.
The original sense was the middle of the day, especially noon. The meal sense developed because the day's main meal was traditionally eaten around this time. Although the meal gradually moved to later in the afternoon or evening, especially as working patterns changed, the old name remained.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk middag, Danish middag and Swedish middag (“midday; dinner”), Faroese middagur and Icelandic miðdegi

1004349.etyen:
Ultimately unknown.
The river's original name is reconstructed as Old Norse *Ork. The present form Orkla may have developed from the name of its source lake, Orkelsjøen, whose older form is reconstructed as *Orkill or *Orkull. The older river name has traditionally been connected with orka (“to work, labour”), perhaps referring to the river's strong current, but it has alternatively been interpreted as an Old European river name; both explanations are uncertain.
Compare Orkanger, Orkdal, Orkland and Orkelsjøen, which preserve or are formed from the same river-name element.

From De (“the”) + store (“large, great”) + Antiller (“the Antilles”), literally “the large Antilles”.
The second element, store (“large, great”), is the definite and plural form of stor (“large, great”). It is inherited from Old Norse stórr (“large, great”), from Proto-Germanic *stōraz (“large, great”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-u-ro-s (“large, thick”). Cognates include Norwegian Nynorsk stor, Danish stor, Swedish stor, Icelandic stór and Faroese stórur (“large, great”).
The final element is the form Antiller, used in standardized fixed geographical names beginning with an art

1005117.etyen:
Compound of Gess-dur (“G-flat major”) + akkord (“chord”), literally “G-flat-major chord”.
The first element Gess-dur (“G-flat major”) contains Gess (“G-flat”), analyzed by NAOB as g (“G”) + -ess (“flat-note-forming suffix”), and dur (“major”). The latter is via German Dur (“major”) from Middle High German bēdūre (“B-natural; hard B”), from Medieval Latin b durum (“hard B”); the adjective is from Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, far”), from the root *dweh₂- (“far, long”).
The second element akkord (“chord”) is from French accord
